## THE CURRENT MAP
2:16/q01 Who are 'those' in this verse? [أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ · referent] (turns on: Whether context limits the group.)
  2:16/q01/p1 The hypocrites described above. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān traces their false reform and mockery; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr favor the immediate context of 2:8 onward.
  2:16/q01/p2 The People of the Book, especially Jews expecting Muhammad. — reasons: Qatāda, al-Suddī and Muqātil are cited; Abū Ḥayyān notes concern for status and income. Al-Ālūsī calls this distant as an occasion.
  2:16/q01/p3 All unbelievers. — reasons: Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās are cited; al-Ālūsī allows general application but rejects this as intended referent.
  2:16/q01/p4 A people described before they existed. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān reports divine disclosure of future unseen knowledge.
2:16/q02 What does the demonstrative and relative description convey? [أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the demonstrative itself conveys contempt.)
  2:16/q02/p1 They mark extreme evil and concentrate the group's traits. — reasons: Bursevī sees exceptional evil; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say the relative clause restricts the description rhetorically, despite other sinners.
  2:16/q02/p2 The demonstrative makes the described class vivid, without inherent contempt. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the far demonstrative for the Qurʾān's grandeur at 2:2 and Qays's near demonstrative for distant death.
2:16/q03 How is the opening nominal sentence parsed? [أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ · grammar] (turns on: Whether الذين is predicate or modifier.)
  2:16/q03/p1 أولئك is subject and الذين with its relative clause is predicate. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn agree. The alternative lacks a linking pronoun and strains definiteness and the past relative clause.
  2:16/q03/p2 الذين modifies أولئك; a later clause is predicate. — reasons: Al-Nasafī reports this; al-Samīn objects to the adjective or apposition analysis.
  2:16/q03/p3 الذين is a second subject or has conditional force, making فما ربحت predicate. — reasons: Al-Samīn reports and rejects it; Abū Ḥayyān rejects analogous parsing at 2:262 for lack of a linking pronoun.
2:16/q04 What does 'purchased' mean in Arabic usage here? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ · meaning] (turns on: Exchange versus choice.)
  2:16/q04/p1 It denotes exchange or substitution, extended to abstract things. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba and others distinguish buying, selling and exchange; al-Wāḥidī stresses desire for what is bought. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Bashāma and ʿAntara; al-Biqāʿī reports root persistence.
  2:16/q04/p2 It means choosing or preferring. — reasons: Qatāda cites 41:17; al-Ṭabarī adduces al-Aʿshā, Dhū al-Rumma and another poet but says following trade imagery favors exchange. Al-Zajjāj's poem describes adopting Christianity.
2:16/q05 What exactly did they exchange, and had they possessed guidance? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ بِٱلْهُدَىٰ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether prior guidance was actual, available, innate, or only professed.)
  2:16/q05/p1 They took unbelief and abandoned faith. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī gloss guidance as the price. Al-Ṭabarī cites 2:8 against a prior true profession. Al-Jishumī prefers this; Qatāda describes shifts from unity, safety and Sunnah to division, fear and innovation.
  2:16/q05/p2 They chose error although guidance was available, without possessing it. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī describes abandoning its obligation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Nasafī liken availability to possession; Abū Ḥayyān prefers a capacity for guidance as price, not attained guidance. Al-Ālūsī cites signs, miracles and counsel.
  2:16/q05/p3 They believed and then disbelieved. — reasons: Mujāhid is transmitted repeatedly; Ibn Kathīr notes different kinds of hypocrites and 63:3. Al-Ṭabarī cites 2:8 and al-Jishumī rejects this for this passage.
  2:16/q05/p4 Jews believed in Muhammad's advent before his mission, then rejected him. — reasons: Muqātil says they expected an Isaacite prophet and envied the Ishmaelite Muhammad. Al-Kalbī agrees; Abū Ḥayyān mentions status and income; al-Ālūsī cites Torah belief and 2:89.
  2:16/q05/p5 They exchanged innate disposition or sound reason. — reasons: Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī cite a prophetic report; al-Ālūsī replies to the objection that fitra is common by pointing to parental Judaizing and later hypocrisy.
  2:16/q05/p6 They gave up outward profession and worship while inwardly disbelieving. — reasons: Al-Jishumī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr report or develop this. Al-Ālūsī rejects outward ritual as the relevant purchase price.
  2:16/q05/p7 They exchanged the obedience for which God created them. — reasons: Ibn Kaysān proposes it; Abū Ḥayyān objects that one specifically created to obey could not disobey, citing 51:56 and 11:119.
  2:16/q05/p8 They chose punishment and destruction instead of Paradise and reward. — reasons: Al-Jishumī reports this from Abū Muslim.
2:16/q06 What do misguidance and guidance mean? [ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ · meaning] (turns on: Which paired states the terms denote.)
  2:16/q06/p1 Unbelief versus faith. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and al-Suddī are widely cited; al-Qurṭubī cites 41:17.
  2:16/q06/p2 Doubt versus certainty. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān report it.
  2:16/q06/p3 Ignorance versus knowledge. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān report it.
  2:16/q06/p4 Division versus community, or insecurity versus safety. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān lists the pair; Qatāda adds movement from Sunnah to innovation.
  2:16/q06/p5 Worldly life versus afterlife, or Hell versus Paradise. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān lists these pairs; al-Qurṭubī contrasts the trades of Paradise's and Fire's people.
  2:16/q06/p6 Deviation, confusion or destruction, extended to religious error. — reasons: Al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī define deviation; al-Qurṭubī calls confusion primary, citing 26:20, and destruction at 32:10. Al-Jishumī surveys other senses and warns against attributing immoral leading astray to God.
2:16/q07 How is the plural wāw of اشتروا read? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ · readings] (turns on: Canonical ḍamma versus rare vowel and hamza forms.)
  2:16/q07/p1 The canonical reading has ḍamma. — reasons: Ibn Mujāhid, Aḥmad ibn Mūsā and al-Ṭabrisī report agreement; al-Jishumī rejects variants for lacking transmission. Al-Akhfash says the wāw preserves plurality.
  2:16/q07/p2 Some read kasra on the wāw. — reasons: Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar are named; it is the basic two-sukūn linker and analogizes لو. Al-Ālūsī reports kasra on the initial hamza.
  2:16/q07/p3 Abū al-Sammāl Qunb reads fatḥa on the wāw. — reasons: Abū Zayd transmits it; Ibn Jinnī calls fatḥa light but least common. Al-Jishumī fears confusion with dual marking.
  2:16/q07/p4 Some replace the wāw with hamza. — reasons: Al-Kisāʾī compares أقتت and أدؤر; al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, Abū ʿAlī and others object that the ḍamma is temporary.
  2:16/q07/p5 A clipped or lengthened pause pronunciation is reported. — reasons: Al-Samīn reports Abū al-Baqāʾ rejecting clipped vowel; Ibn Jinnī describes glides at a hesitant pause. Al-Kisāʾī's poem restores alif after incidental vowel.
2:16/q08 Why does the plural wāw take ḍamma in the common reading? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ · grammar] (turns on: Plural distinction versus transferred final-radical vowel.)
  2:16/q08/p1 It resolves two sukūns and marks the plural wāw distinctly. — reasons: Sībawayh, Abū ʿAlī and Ibn Jinnī distinguish root or conjunction wāw; al-Fārisī cites 3:186, 102:6 and 72:16. Al-Zajjāj compares نحن; Ibn Kaysān cites ease; al-Jishumī contrasts لو at 9:42.
  2:16/q08/p2 The ḍamma transfers from the lost final radical. — reasons: Al-Farrāʾ proposes transfer; Abū ʿAlī rejects a forward transfer and observes movement only before a separate sukūn.
  2:16/q08/p3 Ḍamma follows from the wāw's meaning as subject. — reasons: Some grammarians say so; al-Wāḥidī objects that agentive yāʾ may take kasra and variant vowels are not inflection.
  2:16/q08/p4 Other vowels arise by analogy or ease. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī compares kasra with لو; al-Ṭabrisī reports Yaḥyā b. Waththāb's ḍamma on لو; Ibn Jinnī explains light fatḥa.
2:16/q09 How is the verb اشتروا formed? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ · grammar]
  2:16/q09/p1 The weak final yāʾ changes or drops before plural wāw and the next sukūn. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī derives ishtariyū; Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains vowel change and deletion; al-Samīn gives two routes.
2:16/q10 How is بالهدى read? [بِٱلْهُدَىٰ · readings] (turns on: Opening, intermediate sound and imāla among readers.)
  2:16/q10/p1 Nafiʿ generally uses an intermediate sound for yāʾ-final forms. — reasons: Ibn Mujāhid and Abū ʿAlī cite Qālūn and Warsh; al-Musayyibī instead reports Nafiʿ opening all. Ibn Khalawayh explains the range of sounds.
  2:16/q10/p2 Ibn Kathīr opens the forms. — reasons: Ibn Mujāhid and Abū ʿAlī report it; al-Musayyibī reports the same for Nafiʿ.
  2:16/q10/p3 Abū ʿAmr uses intermediate imāla at verse endings and opening elsewhere. — reasons: Certain feminine forms remain intermediate. Abū ʿAlī discusses rāʾ before yāʾ and its disappearance when yāʾ drops; two transmitters differ.
  2:16/q10/p4 Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī incline hudā; others open it. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān connects imāla to Tamīm and opening to Quraysh; Ibn Khalawayh says Ḥamza distinguishes final yāʾ and wāw.
  2:16/q10/p5 ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr opens most forms but inclines named exceptions. — reasons: Abū ʿAlī names رأى, رمى, رآه and نأى; he gives junction examples at 17:83, 41:51, 17:72 and 6:77.
2:16/q11 What does the bāʾ in بالهدى mark? [بِٱلْهُدَىٰ · grammar]
  2:16/q11/p1 It marks the price or thing surrendered. — reasons: Al-Samīn says الضلالة is object and بالهدى attaches to اشتروا; he explains 4:74 by leaving hypocrisy for faith and jihad. Bursevī and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ apply the same rule.
2:16/q12 What legal inference is drawn from the exchange wording? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ بِٱلْهُدَىٰ · law] (turns on: Whethe

r it supports agreement by conduct or limits an option.)
  2:16/q12/p1 Mutual conduct can conclude a sale without spoken offer and acceptance. — reasons: Al-Nasafī describes taking an item and leaving its agreed price; Bursevī agrees.
  2:16/q12/p2 A purchase option is barred for uneven units of one kind. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Mālik applying the metaphor to this ruling.
2:16/q13 How does the fāʾ link purchase to lack of profit? [فَمَا · grammar] (turns on: Immediate coordination versus an implied condition.)
  2:16/q13/p1 It coordinates failure with purchase and marks immediate consequence. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī attach it to the relative clause; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the act exposes both failure and lack of guidance.
  2:16/q13/p2 It implies a condition: if they exchange, their trade fails. — reasons: Al-Jishumī suggests this; al-Samīn reports a related conditional parse, opposed by Abū Ḥayyān.
2:16/q14 What does the negative mā do in فما ربحت? [فَمَا رَبِحَت · grammar]
  2:16/q14/p1 With a past verb it negates the act without changing inflection, much like لم. — reasons: Al-Zarkashī contrasts nominal and imperfect uses, notes Ibn al-Ḥājib's contextual tenses and Sībawayh's emphatic mā, then cites 5:19 and a mā-plus-illā counting rule.
2:16/q15 What do profit and trade mean here? [رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ · meaning]
  2:16/q15/p1 Profit is increase beyond capital, and trade seeks gain through dealing. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī cites a poem for tajara; al-Jishumī gives تجار as plural of تاجر. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr give commercial definitions.
2:16/q16 Why is profit attributed to trade rather than traders? [فَمَا رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ · rhetoric] (turns on: Ordinary ellipsis versus attributional metaphor and its force.)
  2:16/q16/p1 Arabic attributes the trader's result to the trade; the traders gained nothing. — reasons: Al-Farrāʾ, al-Akhfash, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and later writers cite sleeping nights, resolved matters, 34:33, 47:21, 2:177, 12:82 and Jarīr. Al-Farrāʾ requires clear context. Al-Jurjānī argues this syntactic figure has force beyond literal paraphrase, with poems about drought and concrete idioms. Al-Akhfash also reports an alternative 2:171 comparison: gods and sheep alike do not hear or understand their caller.
  2:16/q16/p2 Trade's causal or associative relation licenses figurative attribution. — reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī calls trade a cause; al-Zarkashī distinguishes lexical resemblance from rational association, citing verses on caused faith and ruin. Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Taftāzānī treat even the negation as figurative.
2:16/q17 Why does the verse continue the buying image with profit and trade? [ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ · rhetoric]
  2:16/q17/p1 The commercial words complete and reinforce the purchase metaphor. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the end echoes the opening. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Zarkashī and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite poems extending images through nests, silk, birds and lizards. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes a literal companion from a second metaphor.
2:16/q18 What does their failure to profit imply about the exchange? [فَمَا رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether no surplus alone proves loss of capital.)
  2:16/q18/p1 They lost guidance as capital and all true gain. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī names confusion, blindness and fear now and punishment later; al-Ṭabrisī contrasts believers' trade. Al-Nasafī, al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr treat guidance, fitra or reason as capital. Sufyān al-Thawrī cites 61:10; worldly gains are no genuine profit.
  2:16/q18/p2 The no-profit phrase alone denies only surplus; the next clause proves capital loss. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān replies to al-Zamakhsharī that a trader may break even. The second clause completes the thought, illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays; al-Ālūsī says religious trade cannot end neutrally.
  2:16/q18/p3 They gained nothing because they falsely expected reward. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān cites claims of divine favor and short punishment, then a hadith that Ibn Judʿān's generosity did not benefit him without prayer for forgiveness on Judgment.
2:16/q19 Is تجارتهم read in the singular or plural? [تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ · readings] (turns on: Collective singular versus individual trades.)
  2:16/q19/p1 The majority read singular 'their trade'. — reasons: Al-Jishumī notes weak transmission for variants; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī explain the collective sense.
  2:16/q19/p2 Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla reads plural 'their trades'. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report that each person has a separate trade.
2:16/q20 How are تجارة and ضلالة pluralized? [تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ · grammar]
  2:16/q20/p1 Ibn Kaysān allows تجاير or تجائر and ضلايل or ضلائل. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās gives unhamzated forms and al-Qurṭubī hamzated ones; these are lexical plurals, not verse readings.
2:16/q21 What does 'they were not guided' mean? [وَمَا كَانُوا۟ مُهْتَدِينَ · interpretation] (turns on: Faith generally, escape from error, purchase judgment, or divine knowledge.)
  2:16/q21/p1 They remained astray and could not escape misguidance. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī explain escape from error; al-Baghawī offers general astray. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the past form implies entrenched, longstanding failure.
  2:16/q21/p2 They made no sound choice in this purchase or trade. — reasons: Al-Māwardī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī cite the purchase; al-Nasafī and Ibn ʿĀshūr portray ignorance of a profitable route. Ibn ʿĀshūr separates ordinary commercial discernment from religious guidance.
  2:16/q21/p3 They missed the believers' profitable trade. — reasons: Al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī report it; al-Ṭabrisī contrasts the companions and believers.
  2:16/q21/p4 Their lack of guidance was already in God's knowledge. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya permits it; al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān report it.
  2:16/q21/p5 They lacked knowledge of God. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī reports the explanation.
  2:16/q21/p6 They forfeited the capacity to receive guidance. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān uses an absent road sign to illustrate missing means and distinguishes capacity surrendered from guidance attained; Bursevī describes invalidated innate readiness.
2:16/q22 Why deny both profit and guidance? [فَمَا رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ وَمَا كَانُوا۟ مُهْتَدِينَ · rhetoric] (turns on: Intensification, proof of capital loss, or distinct sense.)
  2:16/q22/p1 The pair intensifies blame: a trader may fail to profit yet act sensibly. — reasons: Al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān make the distinction. Al-Ālūsī calls it completion; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it exposes foolish aims.
  2:16/q22/p2 The second denial establishes capital loss beyond missed surplus. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān says no-profit may be break-even; al-Ālūsī says the final clause settles true loss. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it also denies ordinary navigation to their aim.
  2:16/q22/p3 The second denial attaches back to the earlier purchase. — reasons: Al-Sharīf prefers this; al-Ālūsī objects that the order and closeness of meanings weaken it.
2:16/q23 How is مهتدين parsed and formed? [مُهْتَدِينَ · grammar] (turns on: Predicate of كان versus circumstantial analysis.)
  2:16/q23/p1 It is the accusative predicate of كان, from plural مهتديين. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ṭabrisī give the syntax. Al-Ṭabrisī compares complete كان at 2:282. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn say form VIII responds to a transitive base; اشتال is no counterexample because it equals شال.
  2:16/q23/p2 It was originally a necessary circumstantial phrase. — reasons: Al-Farrāʾ says it cannot be omitted; Abū Ḥayyān reports and rejects his reasoning.
2:16/q24 What occasion or setting is reported for this passage? [* · reports] (turns on: General hypocrites, foretelling, or Ibn Ubayy.)
  2:16/q24/p1 It concerns hypocrites generally. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān reports the exegetes; Ibn ʿĀshūr reads 2:8 onward collectively.
  2:16/q24/p2 It foretells a people before they existed. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān reports unseen disclosure.
  2:16/q24/p3 The meeting verse concerns ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and companions. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān reports his praise of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAlī to believers, followed by his claim to have turned them away; the earlier passage remains general.
2:16/q25 How does this verse connect with the surrounding passage? [* · links]
  2:16/q25/p1 It sums up the hypocrites' portrait, explains wandering, and contrasts their end with the guided. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī relates it to 2:15; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the detached sentence restates that ending and contrasts 2:5 and 2:7. Elmalılı says following parables make the loss tangible.
2:16/q26 What broader lesson does the trade image teach? [* · interpretation]
  2:16/q26/p1 Life is a trade whose true gain requires guidance and upright conduct. — reasons: Sufyān al-Thawrī asks everyone to examine their trade, citing 61:10. Elmalılı says religion, sound understanding and honesty sustain commerce; deception fails. Kur'an Yolu says hypocrites spend life, reason and will on error.
2:16/q27 What inward loss does the purchase depict? [* · inward]
  2:16/q27/p1 They squander original light and receptivity, ending veiled from God. — reasons: Al-Qāshānī says knowledge, works, gnosis, wisdom and virtue could perfect innate light. Bursevī cites 83:14–15 and Najmī interpretations of desire and worldly attachment; al-Daqqāq's disciple must first remove love of the world before extra worship.
2:16/q28 Is metaphor possible in the Qur'an, as this attribution illustrates? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether divine speech can use metaphor.)
  2:16/q28/p1 Yes: rational metaphor attributes an action to a related cause. — reasons: Al-Zarkashī reports the majority, distinguishes resemblance from association, and cites Pharaoh, Satan, recited verses and other causes. He notes Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām's work, al-Ḥātimī's etymology and al-Aṣmaʿī on likenesses.
  2:16/q28/p2 No: God has

no need for nonliteral expression. — reasons: Ibn al-Qaṣṣ and Ibn Khuwayz Mindād argue this. Al-Zarkashī replies that it would remove emphasis, ellipsis and much Qurʾānic beauty.
2:16/q29 How is the nearby pronoun hāʾ pronounced? [* · readings]
  2:16/q29/p1 Ibn Kathīr lengthens its vowel with a matching glide. — reasons: Ibn Khalawayh reports yāʾ after kasra and wāw after ḍamma; other readers indicate the vowel without an extra letter to avoid adjacent consonants around weak hāʾ.
2:16/q30 How is the nearby مستهزئون pronounced? [* · readings] (turns on: Full hamza versus lightening or replacement.)
  2:16/q30/p1 The hamza is articulated fully, with a lighter intermediate form also possible. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj prefers full articulation; the lightened hamza lies between wāw and hamza.
  2:16/q30/p2 Its hamza may become yāʾ, while dropping it outright is weak. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj gives مستهزيون and calls مستهزون weak except under a dialectal hamza-to-yāʾ change.
2:16/q31 What do nearby يمدهم and طغيانهم mean? [* · meaning]
  2:16/q31/p1 They mean giving respite and their excess or unbelief. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj supplies the two glosses for the neighboring passage.
2:16/q32 What does nearby يعمهون mean? [* · meaning]
  2:16/q32/p1 They wander in confusion, blind to guidance. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj cites عمه and عامه for a confused person and an anonymous rajaz poet for confused people blind to guidance.

## THE NEW NOTES
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p85/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | In فما ربحت تجارتهم, the merchants profit in their trade; the trade itself is not the agent that profits.
[BAQILLANI:v1p76/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The Qurʾānic description of error traded for guidance and an unprofitable trade is another metaphor.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p373/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A third Qur'anic sense is choosing, as in choosing error over guidance and buying distracting talk.
[BURHAN:v3p354/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The four broken plural forms of paucity and the two sound plurals are inherently paucity forms; other plurals may indicate few or many as context determines, as Qur'anic examples show.
